---
title: "Dominance in stick-breaking rows"
subtitle: "Catalog M-17, M-18, C-16"
description: "Fifty stick-breaking draws under a hyperprior show how often the first piece takes more than half of the stick, and why the first piece is not always the largest."
toc: false
---

Stick-breaking builds the cluster weights one piece at a time: V_k ~ Beta(1, alpha) and
w_k = V_k × (what is left of the stick). The first piece has a special reading. It is the
*size-biased* weight W_SB: the population share of the cluster that a randomly chosen unit
belongs to. Its tail has a closed form under a Gamma(a, b) hyperprior,
S(t) = Pr(W_SB > t) = (b / (b − log(1 − t)))^a.

## M-17 · How often does the first piece take more than half?

Each row below draws its own alpha from the hyperprior and then breaks one stick. The first
piece is in colour; a red dot marks the rows where it passes one half. Press **Redraw**
(or Enter) a few times: the running share settles near S(.5).

```{=html}
<div id="w-ribbon" class="dpx-host column-page"></div>
<script src="../../js/vendor/d3.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/vendor/plot.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/bundles/dominance-ribbon.js"></script>
<script>
  window.__dpxRibbon = DPX["dominance-ribbon"].mountWidget(document.getElementById("w-ribbon"), {});
</script>
```

- **Gamma(1, 1):** S(.5) = .591. More than half of the rows have a first piece above one
  half.
- **Gamma(1, 3):** S(.5) = .812. The hyperprior puts more mass near alpha = 0, and most
  sticks break almost whole at the first cut.
- **Dual-Anchor Gamma(2.32, 1.42):** S(.5) = .398. This is the J = 50 worked example's
  Dual-Anchor prior ([Part 4](../dpprior/worked-example-j50.qmd)), which keeps "about five
  clusters" while bringing S(.5) under its .40 trigger.

## M-18 · The first piece is not always the largest

The same draws again, each row shown twice: in breaking order (top) and sorted by size
(bottom). A red dot marks rows where the first piece to break off is not the largest.

```{=html}
<div id="w-sbrank" class="dpx-host column-page"></div>
<script>
  window.__dpxSbRank = DPX["dominance-ribbon"].mountWidget(document.getElementById("w-sbrank"), { mode: "sb-vs-ranked" });
</script>
```

When the first piece is above one half, the other pieces share less than one half, so the
first piece is the largest. The reverse fails: the largest piece can break off later. That
is why Pr(W_SB > .5) is a *lower bound* for Pr(W_max > .5), the probability that the
largest cluster holds more than half of the population.

## C-16 · How far apart can W_SB and W_max be?

Proposition 1 of the paper turns the M-18 argument into a band. For t of one half or more,

S(t) ≤ Pr(W_max > t) ≤ min(1, S(t) / t),

and the engine also computes the middle term exactly (a one-dimensional integral after the
substitution u = −log(1 − w)). Under Gamma(1, 1) at t = .5 the band is [.591, 1] and the
exact value is .728. As t grows the two tails meet: a random unit falls in a piece larger
than t with probability at least t, so at t = .9 the tails are .303 (W_SB) and .309 (W_max).

```{=html}
<div id="w-wmax" class="dpx-host column-page"></div>
<script src="../../js/bundles/wmax-bounds.js"></script>
<script>
  window.__dpxWmax = DPX["wmax-bounds"].mountWidget(document.getElementById("w-wmax"), {});
</script>
```

The **STAR posterior** switch adds the application's released posterior summaries (paper
Table 5) for the five STAR priors. They are posterior quantities, conditional on the 79
schools, and are read from the replication package, not recomputed. Under the vague
Gamma(1, 1) prior the largest occupied cluster holds .920 of the schools on average and the
posterior probability that the largest population weight exceeds one half is .963; under the
Dual-Anchor prior these drop to .724 and .804, and the alpha-only size-biased probability
drops from .797 to .419.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
W_SB is the share of a random unit's cluster, never "the largest weight". Size-biased
dominance and W_max are named separately throughout this site. These are prior
statements. Stick-breaking rows after Broderick (MLSS 2016; 2012 tutorial), with the
mathematics re-implemented.
:::
